concept.name: Scaling in
concept.definition: Building a position in multiple tranches at different prices instead of committing full size at once - either into weakness (lowering average cost) or into strength (adding as the trade proves itself). It spreads execution and timing risk and lets the trader confirm the thesis before full deployment.
concept.intuition: Splitting a 1,000-share buy into four 250-share steps at descending prices turns one all-or-nothing decision into a graduated one, at the cost of sometimes never reaching full size.
concept.mechanics: Set a target price and total size, then place partial orders at intervals, stopping when price reverses or full size is reached. Scaling in also reduces market impact and helps hide large orders; many traders start small and add only as the trade moves in their favor.
concept.formula: Average entry = sum(q_i x p_i) / sum(q_i); four 250-share tranches at $20.00, $19.90, $19.80, $19.70 average $19.85.
concept.failure_modes: Scaling into weakness means deliberately growing a losing position; if the thesis is wrong, the trader reaches maximum size at the point of maximum loss.
concept.misconceptions: That scaling in always improves the entry; if price runs without filling the remaining rungs, the trader is underinvested in their best ideas - opportunity cost is the price of the smoother entry.
concept.example: An investor wanting 1,000 shares of a $20 stock buys 250 shares each at $20.00, $19.90, $19.80, and $19.70, averaging $19.85 instead of $20.00 (Investopedia worked example).
